title: Separate compilation, object files, linking and build commands
learningObjectives: Distinguish a source file, a preprocessed translation unit, an object file and a linked executable.
Explain how declarations in headers coordinate interfaces while definitions provide function or object implementations.
Describe the compiler and linker roles in a multi-file C build.
Use a shared header to keep declarations consistent across translation units and prevent accidental duplicate definitions.
Interpret common compile-time and link-time failures such as missing declarations, duplicate symbols and unresolved references.
Write a reproducible build command that compiles all required source files with a documented language standard and warning policy.

understand.concept: A multi-file C program is commonly translated as separate translation units. The compiler processes each source file after preprocessing and produces an object file; the linker combines object files and required libraries into a program. Header files usually contain declarations shared by translation units, while source files contain definitions. The declaration used by a caller must be compatible with the definition that the linker resolves.
understand.whyItMatters: Separate compilation keeps larger programs organized and allows unchanged components to be reused. A missing source file, inconsistent prototype or duplicate external definition can cause build or link failures even when individual files appear valid.
understand.analogy: Think of each translation unit as a workshop producing a labeled component; the linker assembles the components and checks that required external connections can be resolved.
understand.analogyLimit: Object files and linkers have platform-specific formats and rules. The analogy does not imply that every source file becomes one object file or that all linkers behave identically.

explain.narrative:
The compiler first preprocesses and translates each translation unit. A typical command such as cc -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -c main.c creates main.o; a second command compiles another source file; the linker then combines the object files. The -c option requests compilation without linking.

A header should declare shared interfaces and normally use an include guard. Include that header in both the implementation file and its callers so the compiler can check that the declaration is consistent. Put one external function definition in one source file; placing the same external definition in multiple translation units can create duplicate-symbol errors. A static function has internal linkage and is not a cross-file public interface.

A compiler diagnostic about an undeclared identifier or incompatible type is different from a linker diagnostic about an undefined reference. The first concerns translation of a source unit; the second commonly means the required definition was not linked or its symbol name does not match. Build commands should list all required source files and libraries explicitly.

practise.guidedTask: Given main.c, math_ops.c and math_ops.h, identify which file contains the declaration, which contains the definition and which contains the call. Predict the result of omitting math_ops.c from the link command.
practise.independentTask: Create a three-file project with a guarded header, one implementation source and one caller. Compile each source separately, link the object files, then intentionally omit one object file and describe the linker diagnostic.
hints: A translation unit is a source file after preprocessing, not an entire project directory.
A header normally declares an interface; it should not define ordinary external functions in every including source file.
Compile each source file with the same relevant language and warning options.
Use -c to produce object files without linking.
An undefined reference is commonly a link-stage problem; an undeclared identifier is a translation-stage problem.
Keep a reproducible build command in the project documentation.

questions.prompt: What does the -c compiler option commonly request?
options: Compile to an object file without performing the final link
Run the executable
Enable every compiler extension
Delete intermediate files
questions.answer: Compile to an object file without performing the final link
questions.explanation: The -c option stops after compilation and produces an object file.

questions.prompt: Where should a shared function prototype normally be declared?
options: In a header included by both caller and implementation
Only in a comment
Only inside the linker command
In two unrelated source files with different types
questions.answer: In a header included by both caller and implementation
questions.explanation: A shared header helps keep the declaration consistent across translation units.

questions.prompt: What commonly causes an undefined reference at link time?
options: The required definition was not provided to the linker
A local variable has a descriptive name
A comment is too long
A header uses an include guard
questions.answer: The required definition was not provided to the linker
questions.explanation: The linker must resolve external references using object files and libraries supplied to it.

questions.prompt: What can happen if the same external function is defined in multiple translation units?
options: A duplicate-symbol or multiple-definition link error
The function automatically becomes inline
The compiler merges every definition portably
The function is removed from the program
questions.answer: A duplicate-symbol or multiple-definition link error
questions.explanation: External definitions must obey the program's linkage and definition rules.

questions.prompt: Why include the shared header in the implementation file itself?
options: So the compiler can check the definition against the declared interface
So the linker can read comments
So the source file is automatically executed
So all functions become global
questions.answer: So the compiler can check the definition against the declared interface
questions.explanation: Including the header helps detect a mismatch between the public prototype and the implementation.
